claims.text: Lattice matching between the oxide and metallic substrate is the primary governor of protective-scale formation, stability, and growth rate in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
Lower oxide/substrate lattice mismatch reduces residual interfacial strain.
Lower residual interfacial strain minimizes crack initiation and oxide-scale spallation during thermal cycling.
The substitutional element X, selected as Si, Mn, or Al, changes the lattice parameters of the CrFeCoNiX substrate.
Changing X consequently changes the lattice mismatch between the alloy and its oxide phases.
Reduced mismatch and strain ensure the integrity and slow growth of the protective oxide scale.
Relevant oxide scales can contain chromia or spinel phases.
CrMnFeCoNi oxidation can produce layered Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides, including Cr2O3, Mn2O3, and at higher temperatures a (Mn,Cr)3O4 spinel-type oxide.
Mn mobility and depletion can promote pore formation and accelerate oxide growth in the CrMnFeCoNi system.
In situ high-temperature XRD can monitor substrate lattice-parameter evolution and surface oxide-phase development during oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi.
The proposed combination of synchrotron XRD and complementary mapping can directly quantify oxide/metal interfacial strain in real time.
CrFeCoNiX specimens are to be studied in a homogeneous, well-characterized, single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
The proposed exposure is 950–1000 °C in an oxidizing or mildly corrosive atmosphere for up to 20 hours.
Alloys having lower measured mismatch are predicted to show lower interfacial strain, greater oxide coherence, slower scale growth, and less cracking or spallation.
Alloys having higher measured mismatch are predicted to show higher interfacial strain and earlier oxide-scale failure.
A higher-mismatch composition or condition is proposed as the control baseline.
The hypothesis is falsified if lower measured mismatch and residual strain do not improve adhesion or reduce cracking and spallation relative to higher-mismatch specimens.
Microstructural or compositional factors other than lattice mismatch may affect oxide stability.
